A backyard lawn swap where the county line matters more than the street

Artificial grass installed on a Four Corners lot costs about $8–$18 a square foot, typically $10–$16, the same range as the rest of Central Florida as of September 2026. What's different here is the paperwork: a permit for the identical backyard can run through Osceola, Polk, Lake or Orange County depending on the parcel, and a full-time owner-occupied home is now the minority next to rental-run villas.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

How a full-time home differs from the villa next door

A large share of Four Corners lots are run by a property manager on behalf of an absentee owner, which makes the ordinary owner-occupied residential job something of a specialty here rather than the default. The scope is identical, sod and a few inches of soil come out, washed crushed rock goes down and compacts firm, turf gets seamed and edged, but the schedule is not built around a booking calendar or a rental company's approval chain. That usually means more flexibility on start dates and a homeowner on site to answer questions about grading, tree roots or where the irrigation heads get capped, which speeds up the parts of a job that slow down on a vacant rental.

Why the subgrade slopes away from the house

Grade comes before rock on a Four Corners lawn: the bare soil gets shaped to fall one to two percent moving away from the foundation, following the direction water was already heading before construction started, whether that's toward a rear fence line, a side yard low point, or a street-facing curb. That fall gets rechecked with a level once the first lift of rock is compacted, since two to four inches of stone can flatten a subtle slope if nobody's watching for it. A lawn shaped this way sends a downpour toward the yard's natural low spot instead of pooling against the house, which is the entire point of doing this step in Four Corners before turf ever gets involved.

The four-county permit question, for a plain backyard

A homeowner replacing a dead lawn behind the house still has to know which building department covers the address before scheduling anything, since Four Corners can put that same project under Osceola, Polk, Lake or Orange County depending on the parcel. None of the four has a synthetic-turf-specific ordinance published as of September 2026, so the review that applies is the county's ordinary permitting for exterior work and any plumbing permit tied to capping an irrigation head, not a turf rule written just for this project.

What 'installed to the manufacturer's specifications' actually covers

Florida's turf rule requires an installation to follow the manufacturer's specifications, which in practice means the seam adhesive, nail gauge, and infill rate all have to match whatever that specific turf product's spec sheet calls for rather than a generic, one-size approach. A Four Corners homeowner switching products mid-quote, say from one backing weight to a heavier one, is also switching the spec sheet the crew has to follow for everything from seam overlap to infill weight. Two products installed to their own correct specifications can still look different once finished, since the numbers behind each build aren't identical.

Say you have a 950 sq ft backyard behind a full-time home

Say you have a 950 sq ft backyard behind a Four Corners home you actually live in, with the original 2005 sod thinned out by shade from a mature oak near the fence line. At the typical $10–$16 range, a straightforward conversion runs roughly $9,500 to $15,200, before accounting for anything the oak's drip line adds to the layout. Because the tree sits close to the work area, the state standard's rule keeping turf out of a drip line without a certified arborist's letter applies regardless of which county the parcel falls in, and that's worth checking before a shape gets finalized. Removing the old sod and grading around the root zone rather than through it usually adds a modest amount of labor rather than changing the material cost, so the estimate mostly still comes down to square footage and access. A wider gate than the standard 36 inches, common on some of the older Four Corners lots built before golf-cart access became a selling point, can also shave a bit off the labor line since equipment moves in faster than a wheelbarrow crew.

Taping seams and anchoring edges on a Four Corners lawn

A Four Corners lawn's seams never rely on nails alone: rolls get cut precisely between stitch rows so the pattern lines up, then bonded from underneath with tape and adhesive before anyone walks across the join. The border around the whole lawn is handled separately, either galvanized fasteners spaced a few inches apart along open turf, or a paver and bender-board combination where the grass meets a garden bed. Both choices exist to satisfy the same standard: an edge or a seam has to survive a tropical-storm-strength wind and the standing water that follows it, not just look tidy on a calm afternoon.

Why a driveway edge is often the first to lift

The seam where a Four Corners lawn meets a driveway or patio takes more foot and wheel traffic than almost any other point on the property, and because that edge bonds to concrete with adhesive rather than anchoring into soil with nails, a skipped or rushed bond there tends to show trouble before the rest of the perimeter does. A lifted corner right at that transition after a season of use usually traces back to that specific bond rather than a problem with the lawn generally. Checking that one edge periodically catches most of what would otherwise become a larger repair.

Soil that changes character within the same subdivision

Because Four Corners straddles the edge between the flatwoods and the Central Florida Ridge, two homes a few streets apart can sit on different soil series: poorly drained Spodosols on the Osceola and Orange side, and the deeper, faster-draining Candler sand as the ground climbs toward Polk (USDA Web Soil Survey). Either way the base is the same washed, open-graded crushed rock the state standard calls for, but a flatwoods lot needs the one-to-two-percent grade away from the house checked more carefully, since standing water has fewer places to go once it's there.

Why rinsing habits shift between the wet and dry months

Care on a Four Corners lawn looks different in January than it does in July: dry-season months call for more frequent hose rinsing purely to manage heat and dust, since there's no regular rain doing any of that work. Once June through September rainy season arrives, storms handle a lot of the rinsing on their own, and the more useful habit becomes checking drainage and edges after each significant downpour rather than keeping to a fixed rinse schedule. Treating both seasons the same, either over-rinsing in the wet months or under-checking drainage in the dry ones, misses what each season actually needs.

Questions people ask

Does it matter which county my Four Corners lot is in if I just want a lawn swap?

For price, no. For process, yes: the permit office, phone number and application portal differ by county, so confirming the parcel first saves a call to the wrong department.

Are most Four Corners residential lots on septic or sewer?

It varies by subdivision and by county; older Osceola-side communities and some rural Lake and Polk parcels run on septic, which means the state standard's requirement to keep the tank's access lid reachable applies to any turf layout near it.
